body.x: On a lunar surface covered in extreme cold, extreme heat and dust, Unmanned Exploration Laboratory took on the challenge by developing its rover technologies in-house.
With lunar delivery costing 1.2 million USD per kilogram, the lighter Scarab lowers the cost barrier to lunar exploration.

The space industry has expanded step by step as new modes of transportation have been added. Launch vehicles opened the path beyond Earth, and the satellites that followed created a new market in communications and observation. The next stage is the rover. While a lander can only observe the area immediately around its landing site, a rover — depending on its specifications — can travel from a few hundred meters to several kilometers on its own to survey the moon's terrain and resources. Building on this shift from a lander's "eyes" to a rover's "feet," Unmanned Exploration Laboratory Co., Ltd. (UEL; CEO Jaeho Lee) is taking on the CES 2027 Innovation Awards with its micro lunar exploration rover, Scarab.

UEL's story goes back to 2017, when it was selected as a family company under the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI)'s STAR-Exploration project — a program in which KARI selects and supports promising companies with space exploration technology. UEL was formally incorporated in 2023 and has focused solely on developing lunar exploration rovers ever since, without diversifying into other businesses.

The challenge was that the lunar surface follows none of Earth's rules. Day-to-night temperatures swing between extreme cold and extreme heat, fine vibration and radiation threaten electronic equipment, and finely ground dust works its way into every gap and wears down mechanical parts. UEL took on each of these extreme conditions and built up its rover technologies in-house, securing core technologies across the body and battery, data transmission and reception, imaging, and the electronic speed controller (ESC). The company has also expanded its business model from rover manufacturing and parts supply to payload services and image-data sales, and envisions eventually becoming the mode of transportation for an "Earth-Moon economy" that extends all the way to resource recovery.

Scarab, which is taking the stage at CES, is a two-wheel rover with a total weight of 2 kg and dimensions of 254 (W) × 285 (D) × 194 (H) mm. Its body is made of Al 6061-T6 alloy, making it both lightweight and sturdy. Even while carrying two cameras, it can accommodate about 300 g of payload, and it is being prepared for deployment on lunar exploration missions planned for 2027 and 2028.

Scarab's biggest advantage is its light weight itself. Based on publicly disclosed pricing for commercial lunar delivery services, sending 1 kg to the lunar surface costs roughly 1.2 million USD on a per-lander basis — meaning mission costs rise in step with a rover's weight. UEL turned this cost structure on its head: by cutting the rover's weight to 2 kg, it can significantly lower the cost burden of a mission while also making use of a large lander's spare payload capacity, which lowers the barrier to adoption for lander operators as well. Scarab is also designed with a top-bottom symmetric structure so that it can drive regardless of which side it lands on after being dropped, and its hemispherical mesh-grouser wheels and circular tail are designed to absorb and disperse landing impact.

The onboard computer (OBC) that serves as the rover's "brain" is also worth a closer look. It integrates control of the camera, IMU, motor, communications, and power systems, supports CAN, RS-422, and RS-485 interfaces, and applies a modular design built on a low-power, high-reliability architecture based on conduction cooling. When multiple Scarab units operate together, the OBC also serves as a communication relay linking rovers in shadowed or obstructed terrain with the lander. This OBC has already been proven in the field: it completed on-orbit verification aboard the COSMIC CubeSat (3U) on the Nuri rocket's fourth launch in November 2025, and will undergo further verification aboard UEL's own satellite, UEL-Y-Sys (6U), on the upcoming fifth launch scheduled for Oct. 7. On the ground, it has also completed thermal-vacuum testing (10⁻⁵ torr, -40°C to +100°C), drop-impact testing, driving tests on an artificial lunar-regolith testbed, and structural and vibration analysis.

UEL holds more than 14 registered patents and has published more than 60 domestic and international academic papers, and has carried out technology transfers with KARI, the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute (KERI), and others. Overseas, the company is finalizing payload plans with multiple global space companies participating in NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, aiming to place its rovers in the spare capacity aboard their landers. UEL is pursuing a 2027 mission with some of these operators and a 2028 mission with a Japanese commercial lunar lander operator. In Korea, the company is co-developing a folding-wheel rover with KAIST, and is a co-organizing and sponsoring partner of the Korea Space Rover Challenge together with the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute, and Sacheon City.

UEL's reasons for pursuing the CES 2027 Innovation Awards come down to three: expanding global cooperation and securing an early market position, having its technology objectively assessed by outside experts through CES judging, and converting a track record that has so far been recognized only within Korea into internationally certified results. Because a proven track record is what determines mission adoption in the space industry, UEL's goal is to get onto an overseas mission early and establish itself as the "first verified micro lunar exploration rover." Starting in 2027, UEL plans to use the funding it secures toward lander payload costs, carrying out a mission demonstration every year, while also expanding its payload and data business by supplying the lunar-surface image data Scarab collects to client companies.

UEL is preparing for this challenge with support from from KimVenturous CEO Hyunsung Kim, a consulting firm that advises companies competing for the CES Innovation Awards on their participation strategy. KimVenturous helps Korean startups enter CES with its know-how in winning CES Innovation Awards and its strategic consulting, and is supporting companies preparing for CES together with AVING News. Over the past 22 years, AVING News has partnered with more than 800 media outlets across 54 countries to introduce Korean companies to the world, and in August 2025 it launched the International Press Club to support Korean companies' global expansion.
